readerTitle: Why orchestras started hiring from behind a screen
caseNote: 실제 사례 (미국 주요 오케스트라의 블라인드 오디션) + 실제 연구 (Goldin & Rouse 2000과 그 비판) + 가상 적용 (회사 안의 팀, 소매 체인)
insight: 공정한 채용은 심사자의 선의가 아니라, 일과 무관한 정보를 심사 과정에서 아예 지우는 설계에서 나온다.
misconception: 경험 많은 심사자는 실력만 본다. 편견은 마음먹으면 스스로 걸러낼 수 있다.

sources.text: Goldin, C. & Rouse, C. (2000). Orchestrating Impartiality: The Impact of "Blind" Auditions on Female Musicians. American Economic Review, 90(4), 715–741.
Jacobs, J. (2019). Blind auditions and gender discrimination (Goldin & Rouse 재분석 비판 글)
Gelman, A. (2019). Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science 블로그의 블라인드 오디션 연구 논의

factChecks.note: '1970년 미국 5대 오케스트라 여성 단원 5% 미만, 1990년대 후반 약 25%'는 Goldin & Rouse(2000) 서론의 표현입니다. 원문 수치와 기준 연도를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
스크린이 1970~80년대에 미국 주요 오케스트라로 퍼졌다는 점, 일부 오케스트라가 발소리를 감추려고 카펫을 깔거나 신발을 벗게 했다는 점은 Goldin & Rouse(2000)에 기술된 내용입니다. 카드에는 'some orchestras'로만 적었습니다. 오케스트라별 도입 연도는 쓰지 않았습니다.
많은 오케스트라가 최종 라운드에서는 스크린을 걷었다는 점은 Goldin & Rouse(2000)에 나옵니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
연구 효과 크기(스크린이 여성 비율 증가의 일부를 설명)는 원문 추정치를 인용하지 않고 정성적으로 적었습니다. 2019년 Jacobs 등의 비판(추정치의 통계적 불확실성이 크다)은 표현 수위를 원문과 대조해 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why orchestras started hiring from behind a screen
body: For decades, top American orchestras were almost entirely male. In 1970, women were under 5% of the players in the five best-known US orchestras.
The judges were world-class musicians who said they only listened to the music. Then many orchestras hung a cloth between the player and the panel.

image.label: A violinist hidden behind a cloth screen on stage
image.brief: 무대 위에 천 스크린이 세워져 있고, 그 뒤로 바이올린 연주자의 실루엣만 희미하게 보임. 앞쪽 객석에 심사위원 3명이 메모하며 앉아 있음. 따뜻한 조명, 차분한 톤. 실제 오케스트라 이름이나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your judges insist they're fair.
body: You run auditions for a major orchestra in the 1970s. Your panel is experienced and sincere. Yet almost everyone who wins a seat looks like the people already on stage.
You want hiring to reward only playing. What do you change?

options.text: Remind judges to focus on the music and trust their expertise
options.feedback: It costs nothing and respects the panel. But people can't switch off what they see, so the same pattern is likely to continue.

options.text: Put a screen between the player and the panel
options.feedback: The judges lose information they never needed, like looks, gender and who your teacher was. They keep the one thing the job is about: the sound.

options.text: Add more varied judges to the panel
options.feedback: A broader panel can catch blind spots. But every judge still sees the candidate, so their impressions still shape the score.

cards.title: Orchestras hid the player, not just the name.
body: Through the 1970s and 1980s, many leading US orchestras adopted screens for at least the early audition rounds. A staff member called out a number instead of a name.
Some orchestras went further. They laid down a carpet or asked candidates to remove their shoes, so footsteps wouldn't hint at who was walking on stage.
By the late 1990s, women made up about a quarter of the players in those top five orchestras.

image.label: Audition hallway with a carpet and a numbered card
image.brief: 무대로 이어지는 복도에 카펫이 깔려 있고, 연주자 손에 이름 대신 번호 카드("No. 17")가 들려 있음. 신발 한 켤레가 옆에 놓여 있음. 사람 얼굴은 보이지 않게.

cards.title: Judge the work, not the worker.
body: **Blind evaluation** means removing information that has nothing to do with the job before anyone scores the candidate.

The point isn't that judges are bad people. Everyone forms impressions from looks, names, schools and accents, often without noticing. You can't reliably talk yourself out of an impression. You can stop it from forming.
Orchestras had an advantage: the job is sound, and sound can be judged without seeing anyone.

cards.title: Two economists checked the audition records.
body: In 2000, Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse studied audition records from several major US orchestras. Some candidates had auditioned both with and without a screen, which let the researchers compare the same people.

They found the screen raised a woman's chances of advancing and being hired. Their estimates suggested screens explained **part** of the rise in women players, not all of it. More women were also training and applying.

cards.title: The famous result is less certain than the legend.
body: In 2019, critics re-examined the study. They argued many of its estimates were statistically uncertain, and that the paper is often quoted more strongly than its data support.

There are practical limits too. Many orchestras removed the screen for the final round, where judges met the finalists. And blinding only works when the job has a real sample to judge. Hiding names from a vague process doesn't make it fair. It just makes it anonymous.

cards.title: Most jobs have a version of the screen.
body: A marketing team inside a large company is filling an internal role. Applicants from other departments submit a sample campaign plan.

The team lead strips names and departments from the plans, and two reviewers score them against the same checklist before the interviews. The best plan comes from someone nobody on the team had heard of.
cards.softwareNote: Tech teams do this with take-home coding tasks: remove names and profile links, then grade the code against a written rubric before looking at résumés.

cards.title: Now it's a retail chain.
body: You run 30 stores and need a regional visual merchandiser. Twelve candidates, internal and external, each submit a photo and sketch of a window display for next season.
How do you run the first round?

options.text: Remove names, photos and CVs, then score displays against a set checklist
options.feedback: Judges see only the work the job requires. You'll still meet people later, but strong unknowns get a fair shot to reach that stage.

options.text: Let store managers who know the internal candidates pick the best
options.feedback: You gain local knowledge of who is reliable. But familiarity can outweigh the displays themselves, and outsiders start at a disadvantage.

options.text: Hide names, but show each display next to its CV
options.feedback: Better than nothing. But a CV carries the school, employer and career path that names would have revealed, so impressions creep back in.

cards.title: Fairness is a process you design, not a promise you make.
body: Decide what the job truly requires, then hide everything else during the first look at candidates.
**Try it today:** take one hiring step you use now. List what judges see that the job doesn't need, and remove one item next time.
